chapters.title: Introduction — A palace in the history of Agira
transcript: Welcome to Palazzo Zuccaro, beside Piazza Garibaldi, on Via Vittorio Emanuele.
This residence has witnessed centuries of life in Agira. It was home to a baronial family, welcomed distinguished guests, and, more recently, has become a setting for gatherings and cultural events.
You can discover its story by looking at the façade, the central balcony, and the plaque commemorating Giuseppe Garibaldi’s visit.
But that story begins long before his arrival.
To explore it, let us return to the origins of the building and the family whose name it bears.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — The origins of the residence
transcript: Local historical accounts trace the palace’s origins to a building from the late fifteenth century, enlarged and transformed over the centuries that followed.
An important turning point is linked to Francesco Zuccaro.

In sixteen fifty-eight, he purchased the feudal estate of Cuticchi, establishing the baronial branch of the family. The plans for rebuilding the palace in sixteen seventy-seven are also associated with him.
The new residence was intended to express the prestige the family had achieved.
It was a home for family life, but also a place to welcome guests, build relationships, and take part in the public life of the local aristocracy.
The changes to the building therefore also tell the story of the family: a residence that grew and evolved alongside the standing of its owners.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — The Zuccaro family and the town
transcript: The history of the Zuccaro family, Barons of Cuticchi and Sant’Andrea, is closely intertwined with that of Agira and its institutions.
One significant connection concerns the nearby Church of Saint Anthony of Padua.
Local sources record the family’s donation of land for the building works of fifteen sixty-seven.
As you walk, the short distance between the palace and the church helps you appreciate this connection in the layout of the town itself.
Just a few steps take you from a noble residence to a place of worship, following the traces of a family involved in shaping the town.
It is a way of understanding the historic centre through the relationships between its buildings and the people who helped create them.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The façade and the balcony
transcript: Take a moment now to look at the front of the palace.
The façade reflects the Baroque taste of its seventeenth-century reconstruction and contributes to the monumental character of this part of Agira.
Let your eyes follow the arrangement of the windows and doorways, then pause at the central balcony.
It is one of the building’s most recognisable features, partly because of the historical event associated with it.
From here, in eighteen sixty-two, Giuseppe Garibaldi addressed the people of Agira.
The commemorative plaque on the façade preserves the memory of that visit.
The balcony thus brings together the history of the house and that of the town: a private space from which, for a moment, a guest’s voice reached the community gathered outside.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The reception hall and its painted landscape
transcript: Inside, one of the main rooms is the grand reception hall, designed for gatherings and formal occasions.
The decoration of its vaulted ceiling dates from a later period than the seventeenth-century reconstruction and reflects a Neoclassical taste.
Its subject has been interpreted as a reference to the family’s agricultural wealth.
According to this reading, Demeter, goddess of the harvest, would represent the fertility of the estates. The river figure at her feet might depict the Dittaino.
This interpretation invites us to look for a connection with the surrounding landscape in the images overhead.
The countryside, the harvests, and the river would thus become part of the residence’s story through the language of mythology.
A landscape familiar to the people of Agira, transformed into decoration and symbolism.

chapters.title: Chapter 5 — A king and Garibaldi
transcript: Among the guests mentioned in local historical accounts is Victor Amadeus the Second of Savoy, King of Sicily.
He is said to have stayed at the palace in seventeen fourteen, during his journey around the island.
More than a century later, on the sixteenth of August, eighteen sixty-two, Giuseppe Garibaldi was welcomed here by Baron Mauro Zuccaro.
It was during this visit that he addressed the townspeople from the balcony, an occasion still commemorated by the plaque today.
These two episodes took place many years apart, at very different moments in Sicilian history.
Yet both help us understand the palace’s role as a place of hospitality and encounter: a residence that welcomed figures whose visits would remain part of the town’s collective memory.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 — Restoration and new chapters
transcript: Between two thousand and one and two thousand and three, Palazzo Zuccaro underwent restoration, structural consolidation, and work to bring its spaces back into use, under the guidance of its current owner, miss Silvana Pettinato.
The work also included restoring the decorations in the grand reception hall and the paintings above the doorways, depicting the Labours of Hercules, by the Agira-born artist Renato Pettinato.
In the years that followed, the rooms welcomed new cultural activities.
On the thirtieth of December, two thousand and twenty-three, the palace hosted the ceremony at which Agira received the flag of the Most Beautiful Villages in Italy association.
In two thousand and twenty-four, the ballroom hosted the exhibition “Fashion in Agira Through Time”, dedicated to the work of the town’s dressmakers.

Alongside the memories of noble families and distinguished guests, other stories now take their place: those of the community, its skills and traditions, and the people who continue to bring Agira’s heritage to life.

chapters.title: Closing — Continue your walk
transcript: Our exploration of Palazzo Zuccaro ends here.
From the street, you can admire the façade, the central balcony, and the commemorative plaque.
If you would like to see the interiors, check for openings during events, or contact the owner to arrange a guided visit.
From here, you can continue towards the nearby Church of Saint Anthony of Padua and the other sights of the historic centre.
